name: Benchmark Stat Band
description: Performance figures with the measurement method printed beside each one, so a sceptical reader can check rather than take them.

content.heading: How fast it is, and how we know
content.intro: Every number below names the conditions it was taken under. A benchmark without its method is a marketing figure wearing a lab coat.

items.label: Cold start
items.detail: p50 over 10,000 invocations, Frankfurt, empty cache.

items.label: Query throughput
items.detail: Single node, 4 vCPU, read-only workload.

items.label: Index rebuild
items.detail: One million rows, measured wall-clock end to end.

items.label: Memory ceiling
items.detail: Peak RSS under the throughput run above.

name: Security Posture Band
description: The compliance and security facts a procurement reviewer asks for, stated as figures with their scope rather than as badges.

content.heading: What a reviewer will ask, answered first
content.intro: A wall of certification logos answers none of these. Each figure names its scope, because a control that covers one environment and not the other is the thing a reviewer is looking for.

items.label: Encryption at rest
items.detail: Every store, including backups and the search index.

items.label: Median patch time
items.detail: Critical CVEs, from advisory to production, trailing year.

items.label: Data regions
items.detail: EU, US, UK and AU. Pinned per workspace, never replicated out.

items.label: Access reviews
items.detail: All production access, logged and exportable.

name: Notification Digest
description: A day's notifications collapsed into one digest, grouped by what they are rather than when they arrived.

content.heading: Yesterday, in one message
content.intro: The alternative is fourteen separate emails, which is how a notification system trains people to filter it into a folder they never open.

items.label: 3 deploys shipped
items.detail: All green. The last one is still inside its rollback window.

items.label: 1 build failed
items.detail: api-gateway on main — the test that failed also failed on the previous run.

items.label: 6 comments on your reviews
items.detail: Two are blocking, four are questions you can answer in a line.

items.label: Usage at 82% of plan
items.detail: On the current run rate you cross the limit on the 26th.

items.label: 2 people joined the workspace
items.detail: Both are still on the default role and have not opened anything.

name: Agent Retry Log
description: What the agent tried, what failed, and what it did about it — the run history a user needs before they trust a second attempt.

content.heading: What it tried before this answer
content.intro: A retried step that is invisible reads as a slow agent. A retried step that is shown reads as a careful one, and it is the same run either way.

items.label: search_docs — succeeded
items.detail: First attempt. 12 passages returned, 4 above the relevance floor.

items.label: fetch_invoice — rate limited, retried
items.detail: 429 on the first call. Backed off 2.1 s and succeeded on the second.

items.label: run_query — failed twice, abandoned
items.detail: Column `renewed_at` does not exist. The agent stopped rather than guessing a column name.

items.label: summarise — succeeded
items.detail: Ran against the two sources that resolved, and says so in the answer.

name: Retrieval Freshness List
description: Retrieved sources ranked by how stale they are, because a confident answer from a two-year-old document is the failure people do not catch.

content.heading: How old the sources are
content.intro: Relevance ranking says which document matched. It says nothing about whether the document is still true, and that is the question a reader has once the answer surprises them.

items.label: Pricing page — 2 days old
items.detail: Re-indexed after the last deploy. Matches what is live.

items.label: API reference — 3 weeks old
items.detail: Two endpoints have shipped since. Neither is quoted in this answer.

items.label: Onboarding guide — 8 months old
items.detail: Predates the current signup flow. Cited here for the account model only.

items.label: Migration notes — 2 years old
items.detail: Superseded twice. Excluded from this answer and kept for the audit trail.

name: Approval Policy List
description: Which agent actions run unattended and which need a signature, stated as a policy the operator can read before anything happens.

content.heading: What runs without asking
content.intro: Approval prompts are trusted in proportion to how predictable they are. Someone who cannot say in advance which actions will stop and ask learns to approve everything.

items.label: Read anything
items.detail: Runs unattended. Every read is logged with the query that caused it.

items.label: Draft and edit documents
items.detail: Runs unattended in a draft state. Publishing is a separate action.

items.label: Send an external message
items.detail: Always asks. The recipient and the full body are shown before you sign.

items.label: Spend money or change a plan
items.detail: Always asks, and the approval expires after five minutes rather than waiting.

items.label: Delete production data
items.detail: Blocked outright. There is no approval that turns this on from here.

name: Objection FAQ
description: An FAQ written from the objections that stop a sale rather than from the questions that are comfortable to answer.

content.heading: The awkward questions
content.intro: Most FAQs answer what the company wishes it were asked. These are the four that actually decide it, including the one where the honest answer is no.

items.label: Is this cheaper than building it ourselves?
items.detail: For one screen, no — build it. It stops being true somewhere around the fourth.

items.label: What happens if you shut down?
items.detail: The source is already in your repository and carries no runtime dependency on us.

items.label: Can I get a refund?
items.detail: Fourteen days, no questions, and it is stated on the refunds page rather than here only.

items.label: Do I have to credit you?
items.detail: No. Attribution is not required anywhere, including on the free tier.

name: Contact Sales Form
description: A qualifying contact form that asks the three things a first reply needs, and says what happens next before you send it.

content.heading: Talk to someone who builds this
content.intro: Three fields, because a fourteen-field form is a way of asking for the meeting twice. You get a reply inside one working day.

fields.name: email
fields.label: Work email
fields.hint: We reply here. It is never added to a list.

fields.name: company
fields.label: Company
fields.hint: Enough to look you up before the call.

fields.name: context
fields.label: What are you building?
fields.hint: One line is plenty. It decides who replies.

name: Upload Requirements Form
description: An upload form that states the constraints before the file is chosen, rather than rejecting it after a two-minute transfer.

content.heading: Send us the file
content.intro: The limits are here rather than in the error you would otherwise meet after uploading. Rejecting a 400 MB file after transferring it is a failure of the form, not of the person.

fields.name: file
fields.label: File
fields.hint: CSV, XLSX or JSON. Up to 50 MB — larger files go through the import API.

fields.name: label
fields.label: Name this import
fields.hint: Shown in the import history. The filename is kept either way.

fields.name: notify
fields.label: Notify on completion
fields.hint: Optional. Large imports finish long after you close the tab.

name: Referral Waitlist Form
description: A waitlist capture that shows position and referral credit, turning a dead-end confirmation into the one action that moves the queue.

content.heading: Join the queue, or skip it
content.intro: Everyone who joins gets a position and a link. Three people through your link moves you up a hundred places, which is the only honest way a waitlist is worth sharing.

fields.name: email
fields.label: Email
fields.hint: One message when your place comes up. Nothing else.

fields.name: referrer
fields.label: Referral code
fields.hint: Optional. Credits whoever sent you, and moves you both up.

name: Pricing Value Split
description: The case for the price, made beside the price — what the alternative costs, in the units a buyer already measures.

content.heading: Cheaper than the week you would spend instead
content.intro: A price defends itself against the alternative, not against a competitor's price. The alternative here is engineering time, so that is the unit.

items.label: One section, hand-built
items.detail: Half a day for the markup, another for the responsive and keyboard passes.

items.label: The same section here
items.detail: One command, and the accessibility decisions are already made and explained.

items.label: Where it stops being close
items.detail: Around the fourth section. Before that, honestly, build it yourself.

items.label: What you are not buying
items.detail: A dependency. The source lands in your repository and stops being ours.

name: Product Spec Split
description: The specification table beside the product image, with the two or three figures that decide the purchase pulled out of it.

content.heading: The numbers that decide it
content.intro: A forty-row spec table is a place to hide the three figures someone is actually comparing. These are pulled out; the full table is still below for the person who wants it.

items.label: Weight
items.detail: 1.24 kg with the battery, which is the only way anyone carries it.

items.label: Battery
items.detail: 18 hours of mixed use, measured at 150 nits rather than at minimum brightness.

items.label: Ports
items.detail: Two USB-C, one HDMI, one headphone. No dongle in the box and none needed.

items.label: Repairability
items.detail: Battery and SSD are user-replaceable. Parts and the manual are public.
